articles.title: As Israeli violence escalates, Palestinian youth increasingly identify as ‘martyrs-to-be’
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: “I want you to drape me with the flags of Palestine and Egypt when I get martyred,” 19-year-old Omar Na’saan told his sister before his last will became a reality at the hands of Israeli forces and colonists on Wednesday, September 2. Na’ssan, who was born to an Egyptian mother, was not the only Palestinian to be shot dead in the settler attack that day in Al-Mughayyir village, northeast of the West Bank central governorate of Ramallah and Al-Bireh. Khalil Abu Alia , the same age as Na’ssan, was also killed in Israeli gunfire. According to media reports , Israeli soldiers not only escorted the settlers while attacking the village, but Israeli snipers were also deployed to the tops of buildings and opened fire on Palestinians who tried to confront the attack. The “martyr-to-be” The last will of Na’assan reflects a disposition many young Palestinian men have adopted in recent years, describing themselves as “martyrs-to-be.” For many, the willingness of Palestinian youth to sacrifice their lives for their homeland seems to have increased in response to the growing Israeli violence in the occupied territory. This mentality has grown stronger in the wake of the three-year genocidal aggression in Gaza, and the failure of the Palestinian Authority (PA) to protect its people from both the Israeli army and illegal settlers in territories presumably under its control, as per the Oslo Accords. Meanwhile, large segments of the Palestinian grassroots believe that the US-backed security coordination process between the PA and Israel has restrained Palestinians’ inalienable right to self-determination and their right to resist foreign military occupation. This right is recognized as legitimate under international law. On November 22, 1983, the United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution 38/17 , reaffirming “the legitimacy of the struggle of peoples for their independence, territorial integrity, national unity and liberation from colonial domination, apartheid and foreign occupation by all available means, including armed struggle.” Read more: Will a new political alliance unseat the Abbas-led Palestinian Authority? Israeli settler attacks journalists in Birzeit Two days before the deadly assault on Al-Mughayyir, an Israeli settler attacked a number of Palestinian journalists in Birzeit town, north of Ramallah. BreakThrough News spoke to journalist Mutasem Saqf el-Hait, who was at the scene, to learn more about the circumstances of the attack. Saqf el-Hait stated that upon arriving in Birzeit, alongside a number of other journalists to cover the demolition of two buildings belonging to a Palestinian family by Israeli forces, a settler appeared with his sheep. “He came from a settlement outpost called Kfar Tarfoun, which was illegally established on the lands of the nearby Atarah village in 2025. The Israeli forces were a distance away from us when the settler arrived alone with his sheep,” Mutasem said. “Upon his arrival, the settler attacked some of the journalists physically in an attempt to expel us from the area. He beat journalists Salman al-Khatib and Diyaa Hoshiyeh, and attacked Mohammad Turkman, a Reuters photojournalist, with pepper spray,” Mutasem continued. Saqf el-Hait added that the attacker later called another settler to the area. Israeli forces also arrived, though only after the journalists had already left. With less than three months remaining before the Palestinian Legislative Council elections and two months until the Israeli legislative vote, security conditions in occupied Palestine are only worsening. Analysts argue that escalating violence by Israel will cast a shadow on electoral processes and influence their final outcomes.

articles.title: Iceland votes against joining EU
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: On August 29, a majority of Icelanders voted against resuming accession negotiations with the European Union. In a high-turnout referendum , close to 53% of the 225,031 participants rejected the proposal, while 47% supported it. Mainstream reports emphasized that the campaign against negotiations focused on issues of agriculture and fishing. At first glance, this aligned the “No” campaign with far-right talking points in the region – reflected in congratulatory notes circulated by European right-wing leaders. According to the same reports, the “Yes” campaign centered on international policy and alignment, apparently suggesting the EU as a path to provide more stability in the face of an aggressive US administration with eyes on the Arctic’s mineral reserves. Read more: Greenland on the chessboard of US imperialism Yet progressive parties and groups also voiced opposition to joining the EU, criticizing the bloc’s political and economic agenda. While some left-wing political figures, like the Left-Green Movement’s Rósa Björk Brynjólfsdóttir, announced they would support new talks – reflecting polls indicating a significant share of their voters planned to do the same – large sections of the parties’ membership did the opposite. The Left-Green Movement’s youth, for example, opposed the referendum proposal. Together with youth members from other progressive parties, the Left-Green Movement youth activists criticized the EU’s harsh economic and migration policies, as well as its failure to act against Israel’s genocide in Gaza. “There is enough information available for left-leaning people to familiarize themselves with what the EU stands for, and it should be very clear that is not what we want,” Silja Sóley Birgisdóttir from the Socialist Party of Iceland told local media . The Socialist Party provided more information on its opposition to joining the EU ahead of the referendum. “The EU is an economic bloc and a union of states fundamentally built on capitalist economic policies, a foreign policy that serves imperialism, militarism, and Zionism, the distancing of citizens from decision-making, and the weakening of independent working-class struggle,” the party wrote. “Within the EU’s legal and regulatory framework, market laws are prioritized at the expense of the public interest,” they added, expressing concern about policies related to public education, housing, and healthcare in case of EU accession. “At the same time, the EU’s legal and regulatory framework further opens the door to privatization, competition, and the outsourcing of public services.” Progressives’ concerns regarding accession to the EU were also based on other Nordic countries’ experiences, where activists and trade unionists warned of erosion of social and labor policies as a result of EU policies. “Any attempt to maintain specific standards for the environment, health, food quality, working conditions and the like is, in the EU’s view, an example of interfering with market forces,” Danish activist and politician Karen Sunds said during a discussion on this topic organized by the Socialist Party. Read more: “We cannot eat grenades once the grains no longer grow:” European peace movements organize against militarization Critics also questioned the argument that joining the EU would bring Iceland more security, emphasizing the bloc’s militarization agenda pursues very different goals from countering concrete threats from the Trump administration. Instead, this line of argument insisted that EU leaders and institutions remain mostly aligned with the US, eyeing confrontation with Russia and China. In this context, Sunds suggested , the EU’s interest in Iceland might not rest on building a more coherent regional bloc, but instead on securing energy resources located in Arctic regions. According to Sunds, traces of this interpretation can also be found in statements by EU officials. Already a year ago, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the following on the Arctic’s strategic importance during a Nordic Council meeting: “Yes, global warming brings new and dangerous risks to the Arctic. But it also brings new responsibilities, and new opportunities. Take critical raw materials. Greenland alone holds 25 of the 34 critical materials that Europe needs – a treasure locked beneath ice and rock.”

articles.title: Clashes reignite in Sweida between government forces and Druze groups
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: At least two civilians were killed, and 10 Syrian security personnel were wounded in renewed clashes between Druze armed groups and Syrian government forces in Syria’s southern governorate of Sweida. According to media reports , the conflict erupted again in Sweida on Saturday, August 29, and continued through Monday, August 31, after the Druze armed group the National Guard blocked roads, preventing students from traveling to government-controlled examination centers north of Sweida. The National Guard, which is affiliated with Druze spiritual leader Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri (known for his alignment with Israel), accused the Syrian government forces of firing a number of mortar shells against civilians. The group further claimed that a child was injured as a result of the shelling. The development signals a continued challenge to Al-Sharaa’s administration to integrate all sectarian and ethnic minorities into the state, though it came one week after finalizing the integration of the Kurds. It also exposes the volatile sectarian divisions in the post-Assad era and jeopardizes nationwide sovereignty, as the possibility of Israel’s intervention under the pretext of protecting the Druze minority looms. Read more: Israel launches airstrikes on Syria as sectarian violence continues to spiral Syria’s interim government completes Kurdish civil and military integration into its institutions The commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) Mazloum Abdi announced on Thursday, August 20, the dissolution of the armed group as an independent ​military force. Abdi also affirmed at an event in Syria’s northeastern city of Qamishli that the phase of integrating Kurdish military, security, and administrative institutions into national state institutions was complete and finished. One week later, Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa issued a decree , appointing Abdi as “an advisor to the Presidency of the Republic.” With the completion of the integration process, curtains fall on the Kurds’ long-held dream of autonomy . However, the renewed sectarian clashes in Sweida, alongside the latest explosions in the Syrian capital of Damascus, and recurrent Israeli assaults underscore the prevailing security challenges in Syria.
